newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Schaeuble stands by strict view of Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Schaeuble stands by strict view of Maastricht.

text.p: Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary head of the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), said on Wednesday Bonn must make sure that European monetary union begins on time by qualifying under a strict reading of the Maastricht Treaty.

In separate comments at a trade union jobs summit in Berlin and in a magazine interview, Schaeuble said Germany could still cut its budget deficit this year below the three percent of gross domestic product limit defined by Maastricht.
He said Germany could not afford to overshoot the exact target -- even if the treaty leaves some leeway -- because that would destroy popular confidence in the single currency.

"We have all said since 1991 that the criteria must be strictly interpreted. A strict reading has been understood by most people as 3.0 percent," he told Stern magazine in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.
"Those who do not want to stand by that any more destroy the basis of confidence in the euro."
The comments by Schaueble, regarded as a likely successor to Chancellor Helmut Kohl, fuelled controversy within a coalition already straining to maintain a common line on EMU.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel was perceived to have softened his line on fiscal discipline after being quoted by British papers saying last weekend "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent".

Waigel has since rowed back towards a tough line on Maastricht, and himself rebuked Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel for public comments that Europe had passed the point of no return and the euro would come on time in 1999.

"I advise my colleague Kinkel and other European foreign ministers to stick to their own task of political union and spare us their advice about currency union," he was quoted by the Handelsblatt daily as saying.
Waigel heads the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Kohl's CDU, while Kinkel is a member of junior coalition partner the Free Democrats (FDP).
Independent economists doubt Germany can hit the three percent target, with tax revenues slack and 11.7 percent unemployment which is failing to respond to economic recovery.
Schaeuble said it would still be possible to reduce the deficit below three percent of GDP this year if economic developments are favourable -- remarks he echoed in Berlin.
"All efforts must be made to fulfil the criteria so that EMU can start on time," he told delegates at the jobs summit.
Countries face strict entry criteria to join currency union, including low budget deficits, government debt and stable exchange rates. Currency union is scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999.
He said the Maastricht treaty as it stands had already been ratified in Germany and that "we should stick to those commitments already made in the Treaty."
He added that public debts across Europe would have to be reduced regardless of EMU and that he saw "no contradiction between the fulfilment of the criteria and the fight against joblessness."
